title: Do Narratives Lead Prices, Or Follow Them? Sentiment, Price Positioning, And Measurement Disagreement In Bitcoin
abstract: Public sentiment indices for cryptocurrency are widely published and read as leading indicators. We test that reading on Bitcoin, pairing an archive-documented daily sentiment series (cryptocurrency wire and social-media items classified by a domain-specific transformer) with the log distance of the spot price from its lifetime time-weighted average price, over 752 daily observations from 2024-03-13 to 2026-06-01. We state at the outset that the first difference of this distance is the daily log return to five decimal places (correlation 0.99996), and we verify that substituting the raw return leaves every conclusion unchanged. Under wild-bootstrap inference robust to the heavy heteroskedasticity of these data, sentiment does not Granger-cause price movement (p = 0.630), while price movement does predict subsequent sentiment (p = 0.001); the lag-augmented Toda-Yamamoto test in levels agrees. The feedback is statistically clear but economically small: sentiment innovations account for 0.6% of ten-day-ahead forecast-error variance, and it yields no out-of-sample gain over an autoregressive benchmark (out-of-sample R-squared of -1.30%, Diebold-Mariano p = 0.385). A second result concerns measurement rather than prediction: two sentiment indicators published by the same platform over the same days correlate at -0.018, and the price-embedding Fear & Greed composite shows far stronger apparent feedback from prices than the text-derived series does. A composite that ingests price partly manufactures the causality it appears to detect; sentiment indices are not interchangeable, and their construction should be read before their coefficients are.
why: Sentiment does NOT lead Bitcoin price; negative result, rigorous

title: Epistemic Calibration and Latency Advantages of System One Probabilistic Agents in Limit Order Book Microstructure: An Empirical and Multi-Agent Evaluation
abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) operating under the deliberative System Two paradigm encounter severe structural bottlenecks when deployed in electronic financial markets: token-by-token sequential decoding induces unacceptable execution latencies (3,500-12,000 ms), unstructured text outputs trigger syntactic parsing failures, and coarse sentiment classifiers fail to identify semantic camouflage in corporate disclosures . This paper formulates, deploys, and empirically evaluates a System One probabilistic decision agent powered by TypeSafe AI's foundation model (jev-1.13.0) and optimized via Reinforcement Learning from Classifier Decisions (RLCD) . By restricting the action space to a strictly typed simplex A4 = {HOLD, LONG, SHORT, CLOSE} evaluated in a single forward pass O(1), the agent achieves sub-second inference (mean latency 241.18 ms, compliance 98.8% . On empirical Level 2 (L2) tick data from Binance Futures (BTCUSDT), the bidirectional agent delivers +739.70 bps net of friction with a Sharpe ratio of 14.92, identifying the critical latency extinction threshold at 1,485.00 ms .
why: LLM vs specialized agents in LOB microstructure; real latency tradeoffs, empirical evaluation.

title: Silicon Cartels: Detector Orientation in Multi-Agent Pricing Testbeds
abstract: Detectors of coordinated behavior are calibrated against a control condition, and in multi-agent testbeds that control is synthetic. A control carrying less variation than the deployment environment reverses the sign of a detector rather than reducing its power: separation stays intact while the ranking runs backwards, so orientation-free summaries report success. Of 313 near-perfect separations across 440 detector cells, 103 point backwards. We derive in closed form the critical control volatility at which a coefficient-of-variation screen changes sign, give the exact counterpart for the standard deviation, and show that no such threshold transfers to quantile-based dispersion. On 280 tabular Q-learning runs carrying no language model, the measured crossing falls inside a band declared in advance and survives cross-fitting. Language-model agents price the coordinated arm below the competitive one, reversing the classmean ordering the condition assumes, so its threshold does not transfer to them at all. Separation and orientation must therefore be reported apart, and a screen checked against its control before it is credited with power.
why: Detector calibration methodology for multi-agent systems; surprising finding updates evaluation practice.

title: Agentic Regulatory Intelligence: A Human-Supervised Multi-Agent System Architecture for Financial Crime Pattern Monitoring and Regulatory Guidance Generation
abstract: Financial regulatory guidance for emerging criminal typologies currently reaches financial institutions twelve to fifty-seven months after a new typology first appears in detection data. During that lag, criminal operators refine their techniques and accumulate proceeds that timely guidance might have disrupted. This paper introduces Agentic Regulatory Intelligence (ARI), a formally specified human-supervised multi-agent system architecture for compressing the financial crime regulatory guidance cycle. ARI defines four coordinated agents — Pattern Monitor (PMA), Typology Analysis (TAA), Guidance Drafting (GDA), and Impact Simulation (ISA) — with typed agent contracts, explicit state-transition semantics, mandatory human review checkpoints, and auditability requirements at every stage boundary. The GDA design specifies an instruction-tuned language model adapted to the identified corpus of 44 FinCEN advisories (2014–2024), constrained by a SAR Reporting Guidance Consistency Classifier. The ISA formally specifies a game-theoretic discrete-choice model characterizing how criminal ecosystems are expected to adapt to proposed guidance before issuance; parameter calibration is explicitly deferred to empirical validation. A motivating case analysis across four documented emergence cases shows historical advisory lags of 3–57 months (mean 22.9, median 17.0 months), establishing the operational context. The architecture is evaluated through a step-by-step scenario walkthrough, a requirements-to-component traceability analysis, and a failure-mode and effects analysis covering ten threat categories.
why: Multi-agent crime detection architecture; no eval results

title: Artificial Intelligence, Model Monoculture, and Bank Credit Allocation
abstract: Abstract: Using data on Chinese commercial banks from 2015 to 2024, this paper examines the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) development on convergence in bank credit decisions. The results show that, after policy implementation, bank pairs with stronger common pre-policy AI capabilities experienced larger increases in the similarity of their industry-level credit allocation. The mechanism analysis shows that AI promotes convergence in bank credit decision rules by strengthening reliance on standardized hard information, facilitating convergence in AI technology structures, and improving bilateral operating efficiency. The heterogeneity analysis shows that this effect is more pronounced for bank pairs involving local banks, smaller banks, banks with greater pre-policy reliance on soft information, and banks facing stronger net interest margin pressure. Further analysis shows that credit allocation convergence does not arise from banks jointly entering new industries, but mainly reflects convergence in lending weights within industries already jointly served, accompanied by greater concentration in individual banks’ loan portfolios. These findings indicate that, while AI improves banks’ information-processing capabilities, it may also reduce the diversity of credit allocation across the banking system. Common model dependence and common asset exposures should therefore be incorporated into the macroprudential regulatory framework.
why: Empirical finding: AI causes credit decision monoculture; important systemic risk insight.

title: Q-Learning for Life-Cycle Consumption and Investment with Unspanned Labor Income: A Benchmark Against Dynamic Programming
abstract: We study how well model-free reinforcement learning recovers optimal consumption and portfolio rules for an investor who receives stochastic labor income that cannot be hedged in the financial market and who faces borrowing and short-sale constraints. This problem has no closed-form solution, which makes it a natural test case between the classical Merton problem, where closed forms exist, and realistic household-finance problems. Using the scale invariance of CRRA preferences, we reduce the problem to a single state variable, the wealth-to-income ratio, and compute a high-accuracy dynamic-programming (DP) reference solution. The reference is validated against the continuous-time Merton solution and, in the limit of deterministic income, against the human-capital closed form. We then compare five sample-based learners against this reference: tabular Q-learning with exploring starts (with ages sampled uniformly or in a backward sweep), its episodic ϵ-greedy version, and two post-decision-state Q-learning schemes that exploit the known one-period utility. Performance is measured as the consumption-equivalent welfare loss relative to the DP policy. In the baseline calibration, vanilla tabular Q-learning with uniformly sampled ages still loses 10.4% after 7.6 × 10 8 simulated transitions. Sweeping backward over ages brings tabular learning to 2.2%. The post-decision learner with a backward sweep reaches 0.8% with 1.7 × 10 8 transitions. Across all methods, portfolio shares are learned much less reliably than consumption, because the value function is flat in the stock share near its optimum. We also quantify the welfare cost of popular rules of thumb. The frictionless human-capital rule, truncated to satisfy the constraints, loses 10.3% of consumption for a young worker with no financial wealth. Almost all of this loss comes from its consumption rule, not from its portfolio rule.
why: RL vs DP methodology solid; household-focused application less relevant to institutional trading.

title: The Agent Payment Stack: How AI Agents Are Rewriting Stablecoin Payments
abstract: AI agents are becoming buyers. They purchase compute, data, search, media, and execution services without a human at the point of sale, and the card and wire rails they would have to use were designed around exactly that human. That mismatch is the central problem. Stablecoins fit machine payments better: they settle continuously, settle in small amounts, and can carry rules inside the transfer. This paper maps stablecoin payments into a five-layer Agent Payment Stack and argues that the missing piece is a cross-cutting AI control plane that makes risk, compliance, routing, and settlement decisions inside the payment flow instead of beside it, with an audit trail at each step. It grounds the argument in the public x402 record and separates what is already live from what is still proposed. Approach. The method is a structured synthesis: it maps the stack, reconciles the published x402 settlement census through December 2025 with primary regulatory and protocol documents, and assesses each control-plane function as live, partial, or proposed. Market estimates are labelled as estimates. Across 143.8 million end-2025 settlements worth about $42.8 million, the census shows a sub-dollar metering economy whose revenue and settlement are both concentrated; independent 2026 reporting indicates that the average ticket and settlement volume have since fallen further. The implication is that the near-term work is making agent intent legible and settlement multi-rail. The result is a plain-language reference for payment providers, card networks, and AI platforms, and a short list of the questions the data cannot yet answer. Key takeaway. The technology works and the demand has not arrived yet. x402 settles a high volume of sub-dollar payments, its average ticket keeps falling, and its 2026 settlement volume dropped sharply. The missing piece is not another rail-it is the decision layer that makes agents trustworthy to pay.
why: Payment infrastructure architecture grounded in x402; design contribution not algorithmic.

title: Agentic Commerce and the Economics of Machine-to-Machine Payments
abstract: We explain agentic commerce as the delegation of payments and other commercial decisions to artificial intelligence (AI) and provide statistics on prices and services from Coinbase's x402 Protocol and Stripe's Machine Payments Protocol. Despite more than 200 million transactions, current market activity consists largely of pay-per-use micropayments for digital resources by a small number of repeat buyers. Although agentic commerce can reduce search and transaction costs, it also creates governance and accountability problems when AI agents make persistent errors, interact strategically, or are manipulated, thus generating negative distributional and welfare effects. The review also discusses regulatory approaches and identifies priorities for AI governance and future research.
why: Real agentic payment economics on 200M+ transactions; analytical not methodological.

title: Loan Approval using Pre- and In-Processing Bias Mitigation Techniques
abstract: The main goal of the project is to resolve the problem of the automation of the loan approval processes as it is fair based on the machine learning methods. Historical discrimination against nominated demographic groups can be enhanced by algorithmic bias in the financial technology, and especially through automated loan approval. The given work is devoted to the urgent issue of creating a machine learning model that will be highly predictive at the same time without being discriminatory during decision-making. We suggest the holistic comparison of the various bias mitigation methods: preprocessing (Reweighing and Disparate Impact Remover), in processing (Adversarial Debiasing) and post processing (Optimized Equalized Odds). The AIF360 framework is used to integrate fairness algorithms such as Reweighing, Disparate Impact Remover, Adversarial Debiasing etc. The system compares all the methods and subsequently prioritizes the top 3 best efficient algorithms and visualizes the trade-off between fairness and accuracy utilizing quantitative and graphical representations, which makes financial AI systems transparent and responsible.
why: Fairness methods comparison solid but not novel; no evidence of real deployment testing.

title: Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting and Risk-Window Identification in the Shandong Electricity Market Using a VMD–Transformer–Kalman Framework
abstract: Day-ahead electricity prices in the Shandong electricity spot market are highly nonstationary and volatile due to renewable generation, load variation, supply–demand conditions, and trading behavior. To reduce forecasting lag, excessive smoothing, and poor tracking of extreme prices, this study proposes a VMD–Transformer–Kalman framework. Variational mode decomposition extracts multi-scale price components, the Transformer learns longrange dependencies among historical prices, system operation variables, and temporal features, and horizonspecific Kalman filters dynamically correct forecast residuals. Experiments on Shandong day-ahead market data show that the proposed model achieves an MAE of 68.339 CNY/MWh, an RMSE of 95.404 CNY/MWh, and an R²of 0.701. It yields the lowest MAE among all benchmark models, while its RMSE and R²are close to the best results. Ablation and scenario analyses confirm its effectiveness under high-price, sharp hourly fluctuation, and frequent direction-reversal conditions. The risk-window priority identification rates for high-price and highvolatility risks reach 0.624 and 0.445, respectively. The framework therefore combines accurate forecasting with effective high-risk window identification for electricity market risk monitoring and early warning.
why: Solid commodity price forecasting, typical predictor trap

title: Dubstrata Causal-FM: A Bi-temporal Causal Foundation Model with 2D Grid Attention, Prediction Market Forensics, and Knowledge Graph Diffusion for High-volatility Asset Forecasting
abstract: Quantitative risk modelling and predictive alpha generation in high-volatility financial markets, exemplified by Bitcoin (BTC/USD), have historically been constrained by an epistemological bifurcation: numerical time-series models remain blind to real-world narrative catalysts and structural regime shifts, while unstructured natural language processing systems lack quantitative microstructural precision and fail under execution friction. Concurrently, decentralised prediction markets (such as Polymarket) aggregate continuous, forward-looking Arrow-Debreu state prices, yet their raw signals are routinely degraded by uninformed retail noise, Sybil wash-trading, and whale liquidity concentration.
why: Causal FM for Bitcoin intriguing; contribution unclear

title: AGENTIC AI-DRIVEN INNOVATION IN FINTECH: ORGANIZATIONAL INTELLIGENCE AS A CATALYST FOR PERFORMANCE EXCELLENCE
abstract: The ever-evolving world of Fintech is profoundly augmented with emergence of the Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) systems that enable autonomy, self-regulation, intentionality, contextual-intelligence, and proactiveness in financial decision-making by Fintech financial advisory service firms. By embedding cognitive capabilities and adaptive reasoning, Agentic AI empowers financial advisors and robo-advisory platforms to deliver more personalized, data-driven, and strategic guidance in complex financial environments. To analyses relations between agentic AI & Fintech Performance factors, the research examines Agentic AI adoption in the Delhi-NCR financial services industry using the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT 2) framework. The research employs a quantitative, cross-sectional research design methodology SEM through SmartPLS4 on data collected from individual investors—the primary end-users of AI-augmented financial decision-making tools in Delhi-NCR aiming to evaluate key behavioral and organizational determinants of Agentic AI adoption in FinTech-driven financial advisory services. Key determinants such as Performance-Expectancy, Effort-Expectancy, Facilitating-Conditions, Social-Influence, AI Self-Efficacy, Agentic Capabilities, & Trust proved to be crucial in Agentic AI adoption by Fintech financial advisory service companies. Furthermore, organizational intelligence facilitates the relationship between Agentic AI adoption and perceived FinTech performance, amplifying the impact of Agentic AI on perceived FinTech performance. The research enriches the AI adoption body of knowledge by extending UTAUT2 with organizational cognition and agentic systems constructs.
why: Adoption study, not technical contribution or actual system

title: AI-Driven Innovations in Networking, Financial Technologies, and Supply Chain Optimization: Enhancing Efficiency, Security, and Resilience Across Sectors
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has also rapidly digitized some of the most important industries, such as networking, financial technologies, and supply chain management, to achieve optimized efficiency, safety, and stability. The proposed research is dedicated to the creation of an AI-Integrated Framework, which would integrate deep learning, gradient boosting, and recurrent neural networks to optimise the network performance, identify financial fraud, and predict demand in the supply chain. Its methodology implies the use of all fields of data collection, preprocessing, model training, and evaluation of its performance based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The comparative analysis proves that the proposed framework is better than the currently available sector-specific models, scoring over 90% in all the performance measures, and this indicates its ability to provide reliable predictions, adaptive decision making, and structural operational robustness. The results support the hypothesis that cross-domain AI integration improves the efficiency of the system, its resilience, and security, and offers real-life insights. This study concludes that the combined framework may offer a realistic and scaled solution to the development of AI in multiple fields that can close the gap between the theoretical framework and the active functioning of the piece of research. The data integration in real-time, hybrid architecture, and its application in other domains to help validate the relevance and transformative opportunity of the framework can be taken into account in future research.
why: Generic framework, no evidence of results or substance

title: AI Adoption in Financial Forecasting: Effects on Accuracy, Trust, and Managerial Confidence
abstract: The fast pace of implementing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in financial forecasting has changed the ways of managerial decision making, though, there is a number of concerns about the reliability and the transparency and credibility of the AI-based forecasts. Although other works in the area have largely focused on the improvement of technical accuracy, little empirical research has focused on the effects of AI adoption on managerial trust, confidence, and perceived quality of decisions in actual organizational settings. To fill this gap, the current study examines how the adoption of AI can affect the accuracy of forecasts, trust in the systems, managerial confidence, and the quality of financial decisions. The data were collected with the help of a quantitative, cross-sectional design based on the sample of professionals working in the field of financial forecasting in the business entities of corporate, banking, fintech, and consulting areas. The proposed relationships were tested using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that the adoption of AI considerably increases the accuracy of forecasts and trust in AI systems that subsequently affect managerial confidence and financial decision quality positively. This research empowers the body of literature on AI-enabled finance by providing practical insights on the behavioral and cognitive consequences of AI adoption coupled with empirical evidence on the same, as well as offering insights to help organizations implement AI into the financial decision-making processes in a responsible and effective manner.
why: Behavioral adoption study, not technical methods

title: Robust Portfolio Optimization using Tail-Risk-aware Fuzzy Distributional Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This research presents the Tail-Risk-Aware Fuzzy Distributional Reinforcement Learning (T-FDRL) framework, an innovative method for robust portfolio management in dynamic, non-stationary financial markets. By combining Fuzzy Markov Decision Processes, distributional reinforcement learning, and Wasserstein-based robust optimization, T-FDRL tackles uncertainty in market signals, heavy-tailed return distributions, and shifts in market dynamics. It employs fuzzy sets to model vague market data, captures the complete return distribution, and optimizes portfolio allocations to maximize returns while minimizing tail risks using Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR). Tested on historical data from Apple, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft stocks spanning 2016 to 2025, T-FDRL delivers a cumulative return of 1544.21%, an annualized return of 21.22%, and a Sharpe Ratio of 1.60, surpassing benchmarks like Deep Q-Networks (272.38%), Fuzzy Reinforcement Learning (1120.22%), Value-Based DQN (1067.86%), and Robust Markov Decision Processes (652.63%). With low volatility (13.23%) and a CVaR 5% of-1.64%, T-FDRL excels in risk management, especially during turbulent periods such as 2020 and 2022. This framework provides a resilient, adaptive approach to portfolio optimization, offering valuable insights for investors and policymakers navigating complex financial landscapes.
why: 1544% return on four tech stocks, no OOS discipline

title: AI Literacy and Trust in Peer-To-Peer Lending
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) shapes how financial institutions and fintechs manage risk, especially in environments of high information asymmetry. AI-enriched P2P lending platforms leverage algorithms and data beyond the limited information on loan applications. AI can help predict with greater precision the probability of a borrower defaulting on their P2P loan or engaging in fraud. AI can help minimize biases and facilitate inclusion when borrowing and lending among strangers online. Nevertheless, the impact of AI-usage on P2P platforms depends on whether lenders’ trust can be increased and investment decisions can be altered. This study analyzes over 700 lending decisions by financially literate finance students conditioned through testimonials towards pro-social lending on a mock P2P site. Previous research on a mock P2P site finds lifelike decision making and similar heuristics in a general-public and student sample (Gonzalez and Komarova, 2014). Overall, data analysis shows that investment decisions remain deeply affected by behavioral factors rather than AI-enriched credit scores when lack of AI financial literacy fails to increase investor trust. More specifically, loan popularity and gender factors keep persuading investors, and lender projections of financial literacy influence decision confidence even when platforms inform lenders about the use of AI to better measure credit risk.
why: Trust in P2P lending on mock site, behavioral only

title: The Gold Standard for Capital Recovery in AI Infrastructure Investment What Fiber, Towers and Public Cloud Businesses Teach Us
abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving an infrastructure investment cycle of exceptional scale. Whether that investment earns adequate returns will depend not only on growth in AI demand, but also on market structure, utilization, contractual commitments, counterparty credit, technological change and pricing. This article examines which historical infrastructure business models provide the most useful precedents for evaluating AI Infrastructure investment prospects. The fiber-optic communications boom demonstrates that enormous demand growth does not guarantee capital recovery. Capacity became excessive relative to demand at prices capable of remunerating the original capital base, as numerous suppliers competed to fill largely undifferentiated networks whose construction costs were already sunk. By contrast, the U.S. tower-colocation sector has produced resilient cash flows through locally scarce assets, anchor tenants, long and escalating leases, high renewal propensity and attractive incremental economics from additional tenants. Public cloud offers a different successful model: hyperscalers aggregate diversified customer workloads, benefit from statistical multiplexing, control capacity expansion and add software-platform value above raw infrastructure. AI Infrastructure currently exhibits elements of all three models. Long leases, contracted power capacity, prepayments and guarantees make some projects tower-like. Neoclouds and hyperscalers may achieve cloud-like workload aggregation. Yet fragmented build plans, reciprocal financial relationships, uncertain future pricing and a potentially large number of suppliers also create fiber-like risks. The article distinguishes four utilization measures relevant to AI Infrastructure investment: serving utilization, economic utilization, physical utilization and industry utilization. Separating these measures helps identify which party bears utilization risk at different layers of the AI ecosystem and provides a more useful basis for capital-recovery analysis than reliance on a single utilization percentage. The central investment test is not whether AI demand will grow and create substantial value. It is whether contracted and realized demand will grow quickly enough, at sufficiently high prices, for first owners to recover committed capital before contracts expire, equipment is repriced, counterparties fail or competing supply erodes renewal economics. AI use declaration. Microsoft Copilot was used as a research and writing aid in preparing this article, including for literature searches, source identification, drafting assistance and editorial review. Its use was directed by the author, and all resulting material was reviewed, revised and verified by the author. The article’s subject matter, analysis, judgments, conclusions and opinions are the author’s own. The author accepts full responsibility for the final content.
why: Infrastructure ROI analysis; relevant context but not financial ML methodology.

title: AI Infrastructure Investment Thesis
abstract: This working paper reports an August 1, 2026 descriptive baseline of seven observable parts of the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure buildout: compute spending, physical projects, electricity planning, grid equipment, financing, government action, and adverse evidence. The evidence shows substantial announced spending and several contracted or planned large-load projects, but projects at different stages must not be counted as operating capacity. The author applies a milestone framework to distinguish intent, commitment, construction, and operation, then tests risks to demand, timing, overinvestment, and investment returns. The central conclusion is conditional: physical infrastructure demand can strengthen while returns to any particular security remain uncertain. The scores are qualitative judgments, not statistical probabilities; the separate Appendix A evidence register records the current review and should be updated at future milestones.
why: Infrastructure investment thesis; qualitative judgments, not financial ML method.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Aging, And the Macroeconomy A Life-Cycle General Equilibrium Model with Endogenous Fertility, AI Capital, And Longevity
abstract: This paper studies artificial intelligence and rising longevity together, in a life-cycle general equilibrium model with endogenous fertility in which firms accumulate physical and AI capital. Two results do not depend on the elasticity of substitution between labor and AI. The first is that the stationary equilibrium cannot identify it. Holding the AI income share fixed, fertility, hours, the labor share and every rate of return are invariant to that elasticity, and every level is proportional to a single composite, so a cross-section is consistent with complementarity and with perfect substitutability alike. Only the dynamics separate the two, and we solve the model under both. The second is that the elasticity at which automation begins to depress wages lies strictly below the partial-equilibrium threshold of the task-based literature, falling from 3.03 to 1.99 once the capital stock is free to adjust. The young save out of labor income, so a wage-depressing technology contracts the base of capital supply and the adjustment of capital works against the wage rather than for it. The baseline elasticity of two therefore lies just above the crossing, and its long-run wage effect, an elasticity of-0.0015, is too small to sign at the baseline AI income share. At the smaller shares the national accounts support, it is negative. The two disturbances are then mirror images acting on that same price, AI shifting capital demand and longevity capital supply, with opposite imprints on returns and on fertility. Fertility tracks the erosion of the labor share through a coefficient we prove is invariant to the elasticity, so its own knife-edge is the Cobb-Douglas case rather than the wage threshold. The evidence does not settle its sign, which turns on one object rather than on a list of conditions. The direction of skill bias fixes the sign of the labor-share response, through the share of labor income the complemented type earns, and fixes through the same term the sign of the quantity-quality response. The two offset rather than compound, so the fertility response is negative under the direction the equipment-skill estimates imply and positive under the direction the generative-AI field evidence implies. The sign rests in addition on two features of the environment, a positive pure-profit share and its accrual to the working-age generation. We locate these rather than assume them.
why: Pure macro theory, no data, no implementation path

title: Computerised Financial Ratios: A Game Changer on Financial Performance of Listed Consumer Goods Companies in Nigeria (The Ratio Work-Back Approach)
abstract: The increasing digitalization of accounting and financial management has transformed the manner in which organizations generate, analyze, and utilize financial information for strategic decision-making. Consequently, computerized financial ratio systems have emerged as indispensable tools for improving the efficiency, accuracy, and reliability of financial analysis in modern business organizations. Despite the growing adoption of digital financial technologies worldwide, empirical evidence on the contribution of computerized financial ratio systems to the financial performance of listed consumer goods companies in Nigeria remains limited. Existing studies have largely focused on conventional financial ratio analysis with little attention paid to automated ratio computation and the ratio work-back analytical approach. This study therefore examined the effect of computerized financial ratios on the financial performance of listed consumer goods companies in Nigeria using the ratio work-back approach. The study adopted an ex-post facto research design and utilized balanced panel data obtained from the audited annual reports of ten purposively selected listed consumer goods companies quoted on the Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) covering the period 2016-2025. Return on Assets (ROA) served as the proxy for financial performance, while profitability ratio, liquidity ratio, and leverage ratio represented computerized financial ratio indicators. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and panel multiple regression analysis after conducting the necessary diagnostic tests to ensure the validity and robustness of the estimated model. The findings revealed that computerized financial ratio systems significantly improve corporate financial performance by enhancing analytical accuracy, reducing information asymmetry, strengthening financial reporting quality, and facilitating proactive managerial decision-making. Specifically, profitability ratios exhibited a positive and statistically significant effect on Return on Assets, liquidity ratios demonstrated a moderate but significant positive influence, while leverage ratios showed a negative but statistically significant relationship with financial performance, suggesting the need for prudent debt management. The findings further validate the relevance of the ratio work-back approach as an effective analytical framework for identifying the underlying financial drivers of organizational performance. The study concludes that computerized financial ratio systems constitute a strategic digital financial management tool capable of improving operational efficiency, corporate governance, and sustainable financial performance among listed consumer goods companies in Nigeria. Accordingly, the study recommends increased investment in artificial intelligence-driven financial analytics, enterprise resource planning systems, and continuous capacity development for accounting professionals to enhance digital financial reporting and strategic decision-making.
why: Single-country Nigeria consumer goods, no transferable method

title: The Human in the Loop Is Not Enough: Oversight Debt and the Limits of Human Oversight of Artificial Intelligence in Kenya and Beyond
abstract: Law now reaches for human oversight as its answer to the risks of artificial intelligence. This article argues that the answer is real but conditional: oversight protects only where the human has competence, time, information, authority and independence, and it fails silently when any is missing. Drawing on the European Artificial Intelligence Act, Kenya's Data Protection Act and pending Artificial Intelligence Bill, judicial encounters with fabricated citations, and litigation over Nairobi's data workers, it develops the concepts of oversight debt and the double loop. It proposes a sufficiency test requiring deployers to prove, with evidence, that their oversight could work.
why: Legal oversight framework, not technical contribution

title: From Knowledge to Expertise: Human Capital, Artificial Intelligence, and the Transformation of the Work Pyramid
abstract: Mastery in professional fields has traditionally been built through years of repetitive, ground-level work performed by junior staff at the base of the organizational work pyramid. Artificial intelligence increasingly performs many of these technical tasks, raising the question of whether the pipeline that produces experts is at risk. This paper distinguishes technical knowledge from expertise, drawing on the concept of tacit knowledge and Klein's Recognition-Primed Decision model, and introduces a knowledge-to-expertise ratio describing how the balance between technical execution and expertise shifts across levels of the work pyramid. Situating the discussion within human capital theory, the paper treats enterprise AI as a form of capital that competes with human capital in technically weighted roles and complements it in expertise-weighted roles. Evidence from entry-level job posting data, audit automation, software development productivity studies, and workplace AI adoption surveys suggests that automation pressure is concentrated at the base of the pyramid, while augmentation is more common at managerial and executive levels. The paper argues that AI is unlikely to eliminate experts but is shifting demand toward behavioral and judgment-based skills earlier in careers, moving expectations traditionally associated with senior roles down the work pyramid.
why: Organizational/human capital theory; not about building algorithms.

title: AI-Adjusted Inclusive Wealth (AIW): A Framework for National Wealth Accounting in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Because the sustainability criterion is stated in terms of wealth, wealth is the right ledger for the AI transformation, but current wealth accounts do not identify it. The paper's one substantive claim is an accounting identity, the AIW identity, equation (1), which states where the new terms enter an existing ledger. National wealth accounting records, as far as the corpus swept for this paper reaches, neither data and AI capital as a separately identified asset nor AI-induced depreciation of human capital. AI systems and databases enter produced capital, where they enter at all, inside software, valued at cost rather than at an accounting price. Neither of the two frontier human capital accounts separates technology-induced obsolescence: one carries no depreciation term, the other names obsolescence without isolating it. Two rules govern the identity's use: the AIW compilation triple (v, B, π), which comprises the compilation vintage, the asset boundary and the accounting-price convention and without which no term has a determinate meaning; and the two-branch rule, under which the elasticity of substitution governs the magnitude of the adjustment but not its sign. Three disciplines, D1-D3, constrain how δ_AI, the AI-induced rate of human capital depreciation, may be defined: separability from attrition that is already booked, a net rate, and parallel life-year and monetary reporting. Proposition 1 gives provisional conditions, with known gaps stated in the paper, under which the four added terms are additive to inclusive wealth as currently compiled; Proposition 2 gives the unit convention that separates the fourth term from the fifth; without it the two cannot be told apart from data. Two testable propositions and one internal check are stated with provisional failure conditions, each of which will be registered before its test is run. A descriptive Japan skeleton reports an employment-weighted mean task-share exposure of 0.31. A cancellation threshold of 0.2-1.3 percent a year, the uniform net rate of human capital depreciation that would cancel measured growth in wealth per capita, is reported as a sensitivity value. No term of the identity is estimated. Online appendix and data companion: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23038487 (DroR Working Paper No. 1).
why: Macro wealth accounting framework, off-topic

title: The Algorithmic Crowd: Artificial Intelligence, Correlated Trading and the Limits of Institution-Level Regulation
abstract: Separately controlled trading systems can behave lawfully and still create market-wide risk when they rely on common models, signals or constraints. This article examines how UK and EU law allocate responsibility for that problem, which predates AI and may be amplified by more advanced automated trading. Existing law reaches much of the conduct. Firm-level duties can extend to foreseeable market interactions, venues can respond once trading effects appear, and article 42 of UK MiFIR can reach defined practices firms can identify in advance. It does not clearly reach an emergent crowd visible only after lawful decisions combine. The remaining gaps concern cross-firm information, limited scope and early detection. Responsibility should sit where aggregate risk can be seen and coordinated control can be exercised.
why: Legal analysis of algorithmic crowd, off-topic

title: AI-Driven Human Capital Analytics for Enhancing Workforce Productivity in Fintech Organizations
abstract: The fintech organizations are characterized by a fast-paced technological change, digital disruptions, and changing customer expectations. In this kind of dynamic environment, workforce productivity is a strategic necessity. This paper examines the application of AI-based Human Capital Analytics (HCA) to revolutionize workforce management within fintech companies to increase effectiveness. The study focuses on how machine learning, predictive modelling, and advanced data analytics can be integrated into the fundamental HR practices, including recruitment, performance management, employee engagement, learning and development, and retention. With the help of vast amounts of data pertaining to personnel, AI-based HCA systems can provide more data-driven information about the workforce behaviour, talent trends, areas of productivity, and future talent requirements. The research is of mixed-methodology, which involves quantitative analysis of organizational data and qualitative inputs of HR leaders, data scientists, and fintech professionals. It has been found that AI-based HCA is associated with a significantly better quality of decisions made, reduced human influence, and proactive talent practices (individualized learning interventions, burnout forecasting, and real-time performance optimization). Moreover, AI solutions assist fintech companies to match the workforce skills with rapidly evolving digital skills, thus enhancing the operational performance and innovation rates. Nevertheless, the discussion also features such significant issues as the privacy of the data, the problem of algorithmic transparency, the lack of talent skills in using AI, and the danger of being over-reliant on automated systems. The article highlights that the implementation of AI responsibly, ethical governance of data, and human-AI collaboration structures are needed to attain the best returns. On the whole, this study reveals that AI-based Human Capital Analytics can be transformative in terms of improving the productivity of workforce in fintech companies. Through strategic deployment of AI through human capital processes, fintech companies will be able to create agile, data-driven, and high-performing workforces that can go through the digital disruptions of the future.
why: HR analytics in fintech—off-topic for capital markets

title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Revenue Cycle Management for Reducing Claim Denials and Improving Hospital Financial Sustainability
abstract: Clinically appropriate non-charge encounters are lost in hospitals when they are not charged or not provided due to the failure to meet the eligibility, authorization and documentation, coding and payer-policy criteria requirements. Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform revenue cycle management by not relying on backward work queues to optimize work but instead shift it to be prospective-focused and preventive in nature with the reported accuracy failing to create any financial value or the responsible use. This article evolves and establishes an evidence-based model to choose, justify and regulate artificial intelligence within the United States hospital revenue cycle. It summarizes peer reviewed literature, federal government directions, and industry facts; develops a mapping of denial mechanisms to data and interventions site; and offers a model of value linking model outputs tied to the avoided write-offs, recovered cash, lab work, and expenditure to collect. There are four illustrations of analytical concentrations denial, discrimination and calibration, financial sensitivity, and operating thresholds, which have to be analyzed. The main point is that workflow redesign and careful measurements, as opposed to independent claim determinations are the sources of sustainable value. Implementations that are of high value include regulations and interpretable machine learning, position doubtful cases with skilled personnel, maintain traceable evidence about its source and test the implementation prospectively, before production. The models that hospitals ought to consider are those that can be temporarily and payer-specifically validated, calibrated, and be accurate at their operational capacity, net benefit, allow subgroup error exploration, and track drift. Generative models can help with the summarizing of documents and writing of appeals, but the results have to be source-grounded and they must be approved by a person. It provides a phased implementation plan to get ready to the data, silently pass validation, deploy in a controlled manner, and undertake governance. This framework facilitates the reduction of denial and safeguard compliance, access to patients and financial viability. Figure estimates which are purely empirical are clearly illustrative, and ought to be substituted with institution specific estimates, prior to operational or investment decisions.
why: Hospital revenue cycle management; not relevant to financial markets.

title: Technical Debt in AI-Assisted Software Development
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs), AI coding assistants and increasingly autonomous AI coding agents are starting to work their way into programming workflows, assisting developers to create, modify, test, and document code faster and with less human involvement. A faster code generation however, won't necessarily reduce the long-term cost of software development, especially when the code generated adds defects, security vulnerabilities, architectural inconsistencies, lack of documentation, or other maintenance issues. This article explores how technical debt is an integral issue in AI-supported software development and summarizes a body of literature emerging in recent years that tackles the issues of AI-assisted programming, AI-generated code, technical debt, maintenance burden, comprehension difficulties, security impacts and debt-remediation practices. A special focus is given to the multivocal review by Ehsani et al. which encompasses both existing technical debt types that could be exacerbated by LLM-assisted development and new types of technical debt unique to or exacerbated by AI-mediated programming practices. The literature indicates that when the code is produced quickly, it can be diverted from the implementation process to more downstream tasks like code comprehension, validation, refactoring, security evaluation and maintenance. The results of these findings are not from an original experiment, rather they are a compilation of the current evidence and scholarly thoughts. The authors believe that responsible AI-assisted development involves systematic human oversight, automated and manual testing, proper documentation, security validation, architectural management, and intentional identification, monitoring and remediation of technical debt across the software-development life cycle.
why: Software engineering quality, off-topic entirely

title: Powering Intelligence - Asia-Pacific - A Regional Analysis of Electricity Economics, Climate Advantage, Innovation Tax Incentives, Regulatory Risk, Advanced-Computing Export-Control Exposure and Public-Sector Corruption Perceptions for AI Data-Center Investment
abstract: The region divides along a structural line EMEA did not need to model: only 10 of the 14 markets, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Singapore, Hong Kong SAR (China), Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, and New Zealand, have enacted domestic Pillar Two/GloBE rules using the 15% minimum-tax framework. The other four, Taiwan (ROC), China, the Philippines, and India, have not, and the model therefore does not apply a domestic 15% screening step to their local proxy; a parent-jurisdiction top-up may still apply elsewhere in a multinational group (Section 2.4). New Zealand ranks 1st of 14 (score 81.9) under this model, on strength across nearly every component rather than dominance in one: the lowest Cooling Degree Days in the set, the second-highest public-sector corruption-perceptions score among the 14, a low export-control exposure profile, and a reasonably competitive tax position. South Korea ranks 2nd (score 70.6) despite ranking as one of the least attractive APAC markets specifically on energy availability and land permitting, per BloombergNEF's own comparative assessment. Hong Kong SAR (China) ranks 3rd (score 67.3), and India ranks 13th of 14 (score 47.9): India's tax position is an illustrative local proxy based on an assumed Section 115BAA election for this report's modeled company profile (Section 2.4.2), and its mid-table regulatory score and Tier 2 electricity-price sourcing do not offset that.

title: The Architecture of Systemic Sovereignty From the Ontology of Dead Capital to Managerial and Cognitive Singularity
abstract: This transdisciplinary paper cross-examines institutional economics, neuro-ergonomics, and corporate primatology to model a unified framework for systemic emancipation: The Destin Doctrine. The research diagnoses the systemic persistence of "Dead Capital" within post-colonial economies, demonstrating how asymmetric legal frameworks—specifically the unanimity requirement in civil joint possession—act as a structural "bad barrel." This legal architecture weaponizes historical grievances, trapping assets in a zero-sum game of structural paralysis and resentment. To break this deadlock, the paper introduces a radical paradigm shift: extracting physical assets from the emotional volatility of Civil Law into the mathematical pragmatism of Corporate Law. This is executed through Insular Land Securitization (TFI) and the deployment of the DACH corporate model. By sequestering paralyzed land within Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), the framework enforces "Cold Governance"—a fiduciary structure where operational control is completely insulated from shareholder emotion. This renders the land liquid, bankable, and antifragile, perfectly securing Foreign Direct Investments (FDI) against local legal uncertainties. Transitioning from the institutional ecosystem to human capital, the research exposes the metrological obsolescence of standard psychometric tools (WISC/WAIS). Designed for linear compliance, these tools inflict "sequential violence" on neuro-atypical profiles, specifically Very High Intellectual Potential (VHIP) coupled with Dyslexia. Because VHIP brains operate via top-down, parallel matrix processing, forcing them through linear, sequential bottlenecks generates massive metabolic exhaustion and chronic over-adaptation. As a structural antidote, the paper advocates for technological secession via the integration of Artificial Intelligence as a digital "Exocortex." This synthetic layer absorbs the friction of linear execution. Furthermore, the framework introduces "Legacy AI" (IA Héritage) as an immortal, transgenerational fiduciary, programmed to ensure the frictionless transmission of the founder's logical laws and immunize the corporate structure against future human irrationality. Ultimately, by deploying Cold Governance to neutralize institutional friction, and the Exocortex to bypass biological limitations, the architecture elevates the operator to the status of a "Disembodied Architect," achieving ultimate systemic sovereignty.
why: Institutional economics philosophy, pure theory

title: Generative-AI Exposure and structure of work in Sub-Saharan African Labour Markets
abstract: This paper measures how exposed workers are to generative AI in three Sub-Saharan African economies, using household surveys that reach agricultural and own-account workers and the own-use producers outside the employment boundary. Across 24,838 workers in Nigeria, Tanzania and Uganda the mean task-exposure score is 0.072, and 0.090 weighted, on the moderate 2030 Qwen 2.5 ratings, and runs 0.045 to 0.489 across nine versions. Agricultural workers average 0.029 against 0.134 for non-agricultural own-account workers and 0.150 for non-agricultural wage employees. Inside wage work, formal employees average 0.213 against 0.104 for informal ones. Clerical support, the most exposed major occupational group at 0.615, holds 0.6 percent of the sample. Giving employed workers a high-income occupational mix, with their own occupation scores, raises exposure from 0.088 to 0.209.
why: Labor exposure to generative AI, off-topic for finance

title: Geometric validity is not perceptual quality: what deterministic probes can and cannot measure in generated 3D assets
abstract: Geometric validity and perceived quality are different properties of a generated mesh. In pre-registered analyses, we measured how far deterministic, CPU-only mesh probes (boundaries, components, self-intersection, hidden surface, thin walls, roughness) track each, using expert defect labels, human geometry ratings, multimodal-LLM pseudo-labels and defects injected into real scans. Injected holes and floaters were detected perfectly (AUROC 1.000); interpenetrating parts and crossing sheets at 0.940–0.986, hidden shells at 0.811–0.912, thin fins at 0.952 (two larger severities) and vertex noise at 0.753–0.999, though hidden-surface and self-intersection checks also respond to other defects. On 3D-DefectBench expert-agreement cells, a logistic regression on 30 probe features trained only on crowd labels reached a Matthews correlation of 0.272 averaged over three primary geometry defects, against 0.335–0.341 for the best vision-language judges; no paired McNemar test against the four strongest judges was significant, although one bootstrap interval favoured Gemini 3.1 Pro, and form/surface performance was largely explained by generator identity. Assets that crowd workers judged defect-free were geometrically dirty, while strict checks fired on undamaged scans. Within generators, absolute correlations with MATE-3D human geometry ratings were at most 0.2; on 2,797 Hi3DBench meshes, absolute correlations with automated Geometry Plausibility scores were at most 0.111, did not survive prompt adjustment, and reversed for a geometric-detail score. A training-free conjunction of vision-language votes and probe flags raised Matthews correlation in 29 of 36 pairs, significantly in only one. Such probes are useful as validity gates and confound checks in graphics pipelines, not as perceptual judges.
why: 3D mesh quality assessment, completely off-topic
